summaries.example: Imagine a row of falling dominoes. You see one domino hit the next, but Edwards would say that God is the only ultimate cause of everything that happens. The dominoes are occasions, or events through which God's regular way of acting is shown. Edwards also thought that beauty is greatest when people care about the good of everyone, not only their own friends.
summaries.summary: Jonathan Edwards was an eighteenth-century American theologian and philosopher. His ideas joined two main themes: God rules everything, and God's holiness is wonderfully beautiful. Edwards defended theological determinism, the view that all events and choices are determined by God, but he still thought people could be responsible when they act according to what they choose. He also taught occasionalism, according to which God is the only ultimate cause. Ordinary causes, such as heat making water boil, are regular occasions for God's action. Edwards held that physical objects are collections of ideas or sensations and that minds are series of thoughts and perceptions. Because everything depends on God, he called God being in general. Edwards connected goodness and beauty with benevolence, or love for the good of all beings. He thought true virtue includes supreme love for God and that created beauty reflects God's beauty. He also described a spiritual sense through which holy people can recognize the beauty of holiness.
key_ideas: Edwards made God's complete power and holiness the center of his philosophy.
He argued that choices come from a person's strongest desire or reason for choosing.
He thought ordinary objects and minds depend completely on God's activity.
For Edwards, true beauty and true goodness involve loving the good of all beings.
He believed that some people can recognize holy beauty through a special spiritual sense.
summaries.why_it_matters: Edwards shows how a philosopher can connect big questions about choice, responsibility, the world, beauty, and religion. His work also shows that ideas about God can shape theories about what causes events and what makes a person good. Readers can compare his answers with other views about free will, the mind, and beauty.

important_terms.definition: The view that God controls everything that happens, including human choices, while people can still be praised or blamed for choices they make.
The idea that God is the only true cause, while ordinary events are occasions through which God produces effects.
The view that physical things are known as ideas or experiences in minds rather than as independent substances separate from minds.
A loving concern for the good of all beings, rather than concern only for oneself or one's own small group.
The idea that God is the greatest and most complete being, on whom all other beings depend.

questions_to_think_about: If a choice is caused by a person's desires, can that person still be responsible?
Is caring for your family enough to count as complete goodness?
What might it mean to say that the world depends on God at every moment?

summaries.example: Suppose someone has developed a strong habit of acting cruelly. Edwards would say that this habit may causally determine the person's action, yet the person can still be blameworthy if the action expresses the person's own prevailing inclination. He distinguishes this ordinary freedom—acting as one chooses—from libertarian freedom, which would require choices not to be determined by prior causes, motives, or character.
summaries.summary: Jonathan Edwards's philosophical theology is organized around divine sovereignty and divine holiness. His theological determinism denies libertarian freedom, the idea that a person can choose independently of all determining causes. Edwards argues that self-determination would either require an infinite series of earlier acts of will or make choices accidental. Since a choice is the prevailing inclination of the mind, motives and character determine it. Nevertheless, he distinguishes causal necessity from ordinary inability: an action can be necessary in its causes while still flowing from what the agent wants and chooses, leaving room for praise and blame. His metaphysics extends divine sovereignty further. Occasionalism says that God is the only real cause, while ordinary causes merely mark the regular patterns in which God acts. Edwards's idealism treats bodies as collections of sensible ideas, and his mental phenomenalism treats minds as ordered series of perceptions. God is therefore the only true substance and cause, and created beings depend on God as images or effects. His phrase being in general refers chiefly to God as the supreme, necessarily existing reality on which all other beings depend. In ethics, true virtue is benevolence toward being in general, joined to delight in benevolence and supreme love of God. In aesthetics, true beauty is associated with agreement or harmony among beings; created beauty reflects divine beauty. Edwards's spiritual sense explains how transformed people can immediately perceive holy beauty, while sanctified reason explains why accurate religious reasoning requires both evidence and rightly ordered affections.
key_ideas: Edwards rejects libertarian freedom because an uncaused choice would either require an endless prior choice or occur accidentally.
He identifies willing with the strongest prevailing inclination, so motives and character necessarily shape choices.
He distinguishes causal necessity from ordinary inability: being determined does not always mean acting against one's will.
God is the only true cause and substance; physical and mental phenomena depend on God's ongoing activity.
True virtue is universal benevolence ordered by supreme love of God, while true beauty is rooted in harmony with being and benevolence.
Edwards combines reason and spiritual perception: reason can offer arguments for religion, but rightly understanding them requires properly ordered affections.
summaries.why_it_matters: Edwards brings metaphysics, ethics, aesthetics, epistemology, and theology into one system. His account raises enduring questions about whether determinism is compatible with responsibility, whether perception gives us access to an external world, and whether moral character affects judgment. It also illustrates how a theory of reality can influence ideas about beauty, knowledge, and human conduct.

important_terms.definition: The doctrine that every event, including human volitions, is determined by God, while moral responsibility remains possible when people act from their own choices and motives.
The theory that God alone is a real cause; created events are occasions on which God produces effects according to established regularities.
The view that bodies exist as sensible ideas or perceptions in consciousness rather than as independently existing material substances.
The claim that minds are organized series of perceptions, not substances possessing causal power independently of God's sustaining activity.
Edwards's term for God as the supreme reality and source on which every created being depends.
A disposition to promote the good of being as a whole, rather than merely the interests of oneself, one's family, or another limited group.
Edwards's account of a non-inferential, affective awareness of the beauty of holiness, available to those whose character has been spiritually transformed.

questions_to_think_about: Does acting according to one's strongest desire provide enough freedom for moral responsibility?
What is gained, and what may be lost, by treating ordinary causes as regular occasions of divine action?
Can a theory of beauty based on benevolence explain the beauty of art and nature as well as moral beauty?
If spiritual understanding depends on a transformed character, how could people with different characters disagree about religious truth?

summaries.example: Think about choosing between helping a classmate and keeping all your free time for yourself. Edwards would ask which desire is strongest at the moment. If your strongest inclination is to help, your choice follows that inclination. He would still call it your choice, even though your character, feelings, and reasons helped cause it. For him, being free usually means acting as you choose, not making a choice with no cause at all.
summaries.summary: Jonathan Edwards developed a Christian philosophy centered on God's complete sovereignty and the beauty of God's holiness. His view of freedom is controversial because he defends theological determinism: God determines all events, including human choices. Edwards criticizes libertarianism, which says a free choice must be independent of prior causes. He argues that such a choice would either need another choice to explain it forever or would happen randomly. Instead, he identifies choosing with the strongest inclination or motive in a person's mind. He believes this kind of determination can still allow responsibility because people act from their own desires, reasons, and character. Edwards's metaphysics also gives God the deepest role in reality. Occasionalism says that God is the only real cause, while ordinary causes are events that regularly accompany God's action. His idealism says physical things are collections of sensible ideas, and his account of minds describes them as connected perceptions. God is being in general because every created thing depends on God for its existence and qualities. Edwards's ethical theory says true virtue is benevolence toward being as a whole, not merely affection for one's own group. His aesthetic theory links true beauty with agreement, harmony, and benevolence. He also describes a spiritual sense through which spiritually renewed people can recognize the beauty of holiness. Reason can support religious belief, but Edwards thinks people understand religious evidence more accurately when their affections are properly ordered.
key_ideas: Edwards argues against libertarian free will, but he does not think determinism removes all responsibility.
He says choices result from the strongest motive or inclination in a person's mind.
God's action explains both why events occur and why the world follows regular laws.
God is the deepest reality, while created minds and bodies depend on God.
Real virtue reaches beyond private loyalties toward the good of being as a whole.
Edwards connects moral goodness with beauty and says spiritual understanding helps people recognize holy beauty.
summaries.why_it_matters: Edwards's ideas help explain how religious beliefs can shape answers to philosophical questions about free will, causation, the mind, knowledge, goodness, and beauty. His work gives students a clear example of a complete philosophical system in which views about God connect to views about human choices and moral life.

important_terms.definition: The view that God determines everything that happens, including human decisions, while people may still be responsible for actions that express their own choices.
The belief that God is the only ultimate cause; other events are occasions that follow regular patterns God establishes.
The idea that physical objects are known as ideas or perceptions in minds, rather than as completely independent material things.
The view that a mind is a connected series of thoughts and perceptions instead of a separate mental substance with its own independent causal power.
Edwards's name for God as the highest reality and the source on which all other things depend.
Concern for the good of all beings, not only for yourself or a limited group such as your family or nation.
A direct awareness of the beauty of holiness that Edwards associates with people whose spiritual character has been renewed.

questions_to_think_about: Would you feel responsible for a decision if your strongest desire caused it?
How is Edwards's idea of freedom different from the idea of being able to choose either option in exactly the same circumstances?
Can loyalty to friends or family become unfair if it ignores the good of everyone else?
Why might Edwards think that becoming a better person changes how someone understands religion?
